extracted.intended_audience: students and readers learning formal sentential (propositional) logic (undergraduate/introductory graduate)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules, algorithms, and metatheorems for forming, recognizing, and uniquely decomposing well-formed formulas (wffs) in sentential logic; includes induction/recursion methods for defining functions on wffs and the relation between wffs and Boolean functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 13A — Balanced parentheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Every wff has the same number of left as right parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is stated as a necessary structural property of well-formed formulas; it is used to justify scanning for balanced subexpressions in the parsing algorithm. (Mentioned as done earlier in Section 1.1.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 13B — Proper initial segments are left-heavy
rubrics_metrics.description: Any proper initial segment of a wff contains an excess of left parentheses. Thus no proper initial segment of a wff can itself be a wff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by induction on the construction of wffs. Used to rule out certain ambiguous decompositions (prevents a balanced proper initial segment). This lemma underpins uniqueness arguments in the parsing algorithm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parsing algorithm for recognizing wffs and constructing their tree
rubrics_metrics.description: A four-step top-down procedure that, given an expression, decides whether it is a legal wff and, if so, constructs the unique construction tree showing how it was built from sentence symbols by formula-building operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps: (1) If all minimal vertices are sentence symbols, done. (2) A minimal non-sentence expression must begin with '('; if second symbol is '¬' jump to step 4. (3) Scan left until reaching the first balanced nonempty expression α; that α is the left constituent, the next symbol must be a binary connective (∧,∨,→,↔), and the remainder must be β) yielding right constituent β; create two child vertices. (4) For (¬ β) create one child with β. Footnotes: if required symbols or balances are not found, reject as non-wff and halt. Correctness comments: algorithm halts (depth bounded by length), choices are forced by Lemmas 13A/13B (uniqueness), rejection implies non-wff, successful construction shows expression is a wff by inductive reconstruction up the tree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of parsing choices (forced constituents and principal connective)
rubrics_metrics.description: At points where the parser chooses a constituent α or a principal connective, that choice is inevitable: α cannot be shorter (would be unbalanced per Lemma 13A) nor longer (would create a balanced proper initial segment per Lemma 13B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This argument guarantees that the algorithm constructs the only possible tree for a given wff, establishing 'unique readability' (unique decomposition) without changing notation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Termination/halting of the parsing algorithm
rubrics_metrics.description: Given any expression, the parsing procedure halts after a finite number of steps because each new vertex contains a strictly shorter expression than the one above it; hence tree depth is bounded by the length of the input expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is used to assure the algorithm is effective in deciding wff-hood and constructing the tree in finite time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polish (prefix) notation as unambiguous alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: Polish notation (e.g., ∧αβ for (α ∧ β), ¬α for (¬ α)) can avoid both ambiguity and parentheses; P-wffs are generated by prefix operations D¬, D∧, D∨, D→, D↔.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polish notation has unique readability as well but requires its own parsing algorithm; it is especially well suited to automatic processing (used by compilers). Example: → ∧A D∨ ¬B ↔CB. A unique readability theorem for such expressions is addressed later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventions for omitting parentheses in informal wff notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for writing wffs more compactly by omitting certain parentheses: (1) outermost parentheses may be omitted; (2) negation applies to as little as possible (¬ A ∧ B means (¬A) ∧ B); (3) conjunction/disjunction apply to as little as possible given (2); (4) repetition of the same connective groups to the right (α ∧ β ∧ γ is α ∧ (β ∧ γ), α → β → γ is α → (β → γ)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These conventions sacrifice the earlier strict naming of expressions but are acceptable because we only consider well-formed formulas. Examples illustrate how A ∧ B → ¬ C ∨ D is parsed under these conventions as ((A ∧ B) → ((¬ C) ∨ D)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction principle for sets generated by operations
rubrics_metrics.description: If C is the set generated from initial set B by operations F (e.g., binary f and unary g), then any subset S of C that includes B and is closed under the operations must equal C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two equivalent constructions of C are given: top-down as intersection of all inductive supersets of B and bottom-up via construction sequences and levels Cn with C = ⋃n Cn. The induction principle is used to prove structural properties (e.g., Lemma 13B) and to show membership/closure facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free generation (freeness) conditions for recursive definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: C is freely generated from B by operations f and g iff fC and gC (restrictions to C) are one-to-one and the ranges of fC, gC, and B are pairwise disjoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freeness avoids conflicts when defining functions recursively on C. The recursion theorem requires these freeness conditions to guarantee existence and uniqueness of extensions of maps h:B→V to h:C→V satisfying specified equations for f and g.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recursion theorem — existence and uniqueness of recursively defined functions on freely generated sets
rubrics_metrics.description: If C is freely generated from B by operations f and g, and V with operations F and G is given along with h:B→V, then there is a unique h:C→V such that h(b)=h(b) for b∈B and h(f(x,y))=F(h(x),h(y)), h(g(x))=G(h(x)) for x,y∈C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof constructs h as the union of all 'acceptable' partial functions and shows h is single-valued, acceptable, has domain C (uses freeness), and is unique. Illustrative chromatic metaphor: coloring initial elements and specifying how colors combine under operations. Counterexample demonstrates failure if freeness conditions do not hold (e.g., conflicting equations for naturals with arithmetic operations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unique Readability Theorem for wffs (freeness of wff generation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The five formula-building operations (E¬, E∧, E∨, E→, E↔), when restricted to the set of wffs, have ranges disjoint from each other and from the set of sentence symbols, and are one-to-one; i.e., the set of wffs is freely generated from sentence symbols by these operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Lemma 13B to show one-to-one nature (no balanced proper initial segment) and distinctness of connective symbols to show disjoint ranges. This theorem is the metatheoretical basis for unique decomposition and for extending truth assignments by recursion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boolean-function semantics and semantic characterizations (Theorem 15A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Associate to each wff α (with sentence symbols among A1,...,An) an n-place Boolean function Bα; then (a) α |= β iff for all X∈{F,T}^n, Bα(X) ≤ Bβ(X) (with F<T), (b) α ≡ β iff Bα = Bβ, and (c) |= α iff Bα is the constant T function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identifies entailment, logical equivalence, and tautology in terms of pointwise ordering/equality of the Boolean functions realized by formulas. Example given: table for A1 ∧ A2 illustrating Bα.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressive completeness: every Boolean function is realizable by a wff (Theorem 15B / Post's theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any n-place Boolean function G (n≥1) there is a wff α (on A1,...,An) such that Bα = G; i.e., any Boolean function can be realized by a propositional formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive proof: if G is identically false use A1 ∧ ¬A1; otherwise list all n-tuples where G is T, for each build a conjunction γi selecting Ai or ¬Ai according to that tuple, and let α be the disjunction of those γi (disjunctive normal form). Example demonstrates the procedure for a 3-place function. This shows that adding additional finite-place connectives (e.g., majority) gains no expressive power since they can be expressed by combinations of the basic connectives (though possibly more succinctly).
